questions: A namespaced request for storage of a given size and access mode, which binds to a PersistentVolume
Pods use storage through PVCs. A PVC is bound to a PV, which is either provisioned dynamically by a StorageClass or pre-created by an administrator.
Correct: a PVC is a request for storage.
Each Kafka broker has a PVC data-0-my-es-kafka-0 of 500Gi.
How volumes are dynamically provisioned (provisioner, parameters, reclaim policy, binding mode, expansion)
StorageClasses describe classes of storage, such as fast block storage or shared file storage, and how to provision them dynamically.
ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd provides block RWO; ocs-storagecluster-cephfs provides file RWX.
Pick the StorageClass to match the access mode and performance needs.
What does the ReadWriteOnce (RWO) access mode mean?
The volume can be mounted read-write by a single node at a time
The volume can be mounted read-write by many nodes
The volume can only be written once
RWO allows read-write mounting by one node, which typically suits block storage. RWX allows many nodes; ROX allows many readers.
Wrong: a common misreading of the name.
MQ Native HA replicas each use their own RWO volume.
RWO is per node, not per pod (ReadWriteOncePod is stricter).
Which access mode allows a volume to be mounted read-write by pods on multiple nodes simultaneously?
RWX is required for shared file systems used concurrently by multiple pods on different nodes, typically provided by file storage such as CephFS or NFS.
A multi-instance queue manager's active and standby pods share an RWX volume.
Which storage access mode does an IBM MQ multi-instance queue manager require?
ReadWriteMany (RWX) shared file storage with reliable file locking
ReadWriteOnce block storage per pod with no sharing
Multi-instance queue managers share data and logs between the active and standby instances, so they need an RWX file system with the locking behaviour MQ requires.
Wrong: MQ does not use object storage for queue data.
The team validates the NFS storage with MQ's file system checking tool (amqmfsck) before going live.
Which storage is appropriate for an MQ Native HA queue manager?
A ReadWriteOnce (block) volume for each of the three replicas
A single RWX volume shared by the three replicas
Native HA replicates data at the MQ level, so each replica has its own independent RWO volume, ideally in different zones.
Wrong: shared storage is not used by Native HA.
qm-ibm-mq-0/1/2 each bind to their own 100Gi ceph-rbd volume.
Native HA does replication itself; storage stays independent.
Which storage type is recommended for Event Streams (Kafka) broker data?
Block storage with ReadWriteOnce volumes per broker, sized for retention and throughput
Shared NFS RWX volume used by all brokers
Object storage mounted as the log directory
Kafka brokers each manage their own log directories and replicate at the application level. RWO block storage gives the best performance and isolation.
Wrong: shared NFS performs poorly and is not recommended.
Wrong: Kafka logs require a POSIX disk.
Three brokers each get a 1Ti RWO volume on SSD-backed block storage.
Which storage combination does the Automation assets repository typically require?
RWX file storage for asset data and RWO block storage for its metadata database
The asset repository stores asset files on a shared volume (RWX) and keeps metadata in a database on block storage (RWO). Check the 16.1.0 documentation for the exact requirements.
Correct: RWX for assets plus RWO for metadata.
assetDataVolume uses cephfs (RWX); the database volume uses ceph-rbd (RWO).
When a capability lists two volumes, check the access mode needed by each.
Which OpenShift Data Foundation (ODF) storage classes provide block RWO and file RWX respectively?
nfs-client for block and gp3 for file
ODF provides Ceph RBD (block) for RWO volumes and CephFS (file) for RWX volumes, and also object storage through RGW or NooBaa.
Correct: RBD for block, CephFS for file.
Wrong: local storage is node-bound RWO.
Kafka uses ceph-rbd; the multi-instance queue manager uses cephfs.
Why is block storage generally preferred over shared file storage for databases and messaging logs (for example the API Connect database, Kafka logs and MQ Native HA)?
It typically offers lower latency and more predictable IOPS for write-intensive, sync-heavy workloads, and these systems handle replication themselves
Kubernetes does not support file storage

Databases and logs perform many small synchronous writes. Block storage avoids network file system overhead and locking. These systems replicate at the application layer, so shared access is unnecessary.
Correct: performance and suitability for sync-heavy writes.
Wrong: file storage can be encrypted.
Moving the queue manager logs from NFS to block storage improved persistent message throughput threefold.
Persistent messaging throughput is bounded by log write latency.
What does a StorageClass reclaimPolicy of 'Retain' do when a PVC is deleted?
The PV and its data are kept for manual recovery or cleanup, instead of being deleted automatically
The volume is copied to another cluster
Retain protects data from accidental PVC deletion; an administrator must reclaim the PV manually. Delete removes the backing volume along with the PVC.
Wrong: the PVC can be deleted.
Production queue manager volumes use a Retain class so an accidental uninstall does not destroy data.
Critical data -> consider a Retain policy.
Why is volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer recommended for zonal block storage in multi-zone clusters?
It delays volume provisioning until the pod is scheduled, so the volume is created in the same zone as the node running the pod
It enables RWX on block storage
With Immediate binding, a volume could be created in a zone where the pod cannot be scheduled. WaitForFirstConsumer provisions it according to the pod's placement.
Wrong: does not change access modes.
Kafka broker 2's volume is created in zone C because the broker pod was scheduled there.
Zonal disks + Immediate binding = pods stuck on 'volume node affinity conflict'.
A PVC stays 'Pending' with the event 'no persistent volumes available for this claim and no storage class is set'. What is the cause?
The PVC specifies no StorageClass and the cluster has no default StorageClass (or no matching static PV exists)
The pod is out of memory
Without a StorageClass, dynamic provisioning cannot happen unless a default class exists or a matching pre-created PV is available.
Correct: no class or default and no matching PV.
Setting spec.storage.class in the instance CR, or marking a default StorageClass, resolved it.
PVC Pending -> describe the PVC; the events state the reason.
A PVC requesting ReadWriteMany remains Pending with a block-only StorageClass (for example ceph-rbd in filesystem mode). Why?
The StorageClass's provisioner cannot satisfy the RWX access mode; use a file storage class (for example CephFS or NFS) that supports RWX
The namespace has too many pods
Block volumes in filesystem mode generally support only RWO. RWX requires a file storage provisioner.
Correct: access mode not supported by the class.
Wrong: size does not cause this.
Switching the multi-instance queue manager PVC to ocs-storagecluster-cephfs let it bind.
Access mode and StorageClass capabilities must match.
After a node failure, a Kafka broker pod is rescheduled but stays in ContainerCreating with 'Multi-Attach error for volume ... Volume is already exclusively attached to one node'. What is happening?

The RWO volume is still attached to the failed node; the storage system or attach/detach controller must release it (sometimes after a timeout or manual node cleanup) before it can attach to the new node
The topic has too many partitions

RWO volumes can attach to one node only. When a node fails ungracefully, detaching may wait for timeouts or need intervention (for example deleting the failed node object or using node fencing) so the volume can move.
Correct: the RWO volume is still attached to the failed node.
Once the failed node was removed (or fenced), the volume detached and the broker started on the new node.
Stateful failover time includes volume detach and attach time. Factor it into RTO.
A pod fails with 'volume node affinity conflict' when it is rescheduled. What does this mean?
The pod's PV is restricted to a zone (or node) where the pod cannot currently be scheduled, for example because that zone has no capacity or the pod's affinity excludes it
Zonal volumes can only attach to nodes in their zone. If scheduling constraints or capacity prevent placing the pod in that zone, it cannot start.
Correct: zone or topology mismatch between the PV and possible nodes.
Adding worker capacity in zone A let the broker reschedule next to its volume.
Stateful pods are tied to their volume's zone. Keep capacity in every zone.
A queue manager's PVC is nearly full, causing log write errors. The StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion: true. What is the supported fix?
Increase the PVC's requested size (through the CR's storage size where the operator supports it, or the PVC itself) and allow the file system to expand
Delete old log files manually inside the container
With volume expansion enabled, increasing the requested size expands the volume, sometimes online. Manually deleting MQ log extents can corrupt recovery.
The queue manager log volume grows from 20Gi to 50Gi through the StorageClass expansion support.
Never delete MQ log extents manually; use log management settings.
A pod cannot write to its mounted volume and fails with 'permission denied'. The volume is provisioned correctly. What is a common cause in OpenShift?
File system ownership or permissions do not match the container's runtime UID or fsGroup assigned by the Security Context Constraint
The CPU limit is too low

OpenShift runs containers with arbitrary UIDs from the namespace range. Volumes must allow that UID or group (through fsGroup or supplemental groups) to write. Some storage backends, for example NFS, need extra configuration.
Correct: UID, fsGroup or permission mismatch.
An NFS export with root_squash and wrong ownership blocked MQ writes until permissions were corrected.
OpenShift's random UID plus NFS permissions is a classic storage problem.
Persistent messaging throughput on a queue manager is lower than expected, while CPU is low. Which storage metric is MOST likely to explain this?
High write latency (fsync time) on the queue manager's log volume
Number of PVCs in the namespace
Read throughput of the image registry
Persistent message commits require log forces (synchronous writes). Disk write latency directly limits commit rate when CPU is not the bottleneck.
Correct: log write latency limits persistent throughput.
Wrong: capacity does not affect latency.
Moving logs to a lower-latency SSD storage class raised commits per second from 1,500 to 6,000.
An architect must size storage for a Kafka cluster ingesting 50 MB/s, retaining data for 3 days, with replication factor 3. Approximately how much raw cluster storage is needed before headroom?
About 50 MB/s x 259,200 s x 3, which is roughly 38.9 TB, plus headroom (for example 30-40%) for growth, rebalancing and segment overhead
About 13 TB, because replication does not consume storage
About 4.3 TB per broker regardless of count

Storage = ingest rate x retention seconds x replication factor. 50 MB/s x 259,200 s = 12.96 TB of logical data, times 3 replicas = 38.9 TB, plus headroom for growth, uneven distribution, rebalancing and compaction or segment overhead.
Correct: rate x retention x RF, plus headroom.
Wrong: not derived from the requirements.
With 6 brokers, each needs about 6.5 TB before headroom, so the team provisions 9 TB per broker.
Kafka storage formula: throughput x retention x RF x (1 + headroom).
Which storage characteristic is MOST important to validate for latency-sensitive integration workloads before going to production?
IOPS and latency under realistic load (for example with fio or product-specific performance tests), not just capacity
Only the total capacity in TB
The colour of the storage dashboard
Capacity alone does not predict performance. Messaging and database workloads depend on latency and IOPS under concurrency.
A pre-production fio test revealed 15 ms write latency, which was unacceptable for the MQ logs.
Performance test storage before production, not after.
Which storage is appropriate for API Connect subsystems (management database, portal, analytics) in CP4I?
Block storage with RWO access, from a StorageClass that meets API Connect's performance guidance (NFS is not recommended for these subsystems)
API Connect subsystems run databases and search indexes that need block storage performance and consistency. Shared NFS is unsuitable for their database workloads.
Wrong: not how the subsystems store state (object storage is used for backups).
API Connect uses ceph-rbd for its volumes and S3-compatible storage as its backup target.
Databases on block storage; backups to object storage.
Which TWO statements about storage planning for a production CP4I cluster are correct? (Select TWO.)
Identify each capability's access mode and performance needs (for example RWO block for Kafka and Native HA, RWX file for multi-instance MQ and asset data)
Provide storage that is available in every zone where stateful pods may run, so zonal failover is possible
Use a single local disk on one node for all workloads
Avoid persistent storage for queue managers to simplify upgrades
Production storage planning maps each workload's access mode and performance needs to storage classes, and ensures zone availability so replicas can run in every zone.
Correct: match capabilities to storage types.
Wrong: a single point of failure.
The storage plan lists each CP4I component, its access mode, size, class and backup approach.
Build a storage matrix per capability as part of the solution design.
An organization's only available storage is an enterprise NFS array (no block storage). Which CP4I components are MOST at risk, and what should the architect do?

Components needing block-like performance or sync-heavy writes (Kafka brokers, API Connect databases, MQ Native HA logs) are at risk; introduce a supported block storage option (for example ODF, a CSI block driver, or cloud block volumes) before production
Only the Platform UI is affected

NFS can serve RWX needs such as multi-instance MQ (with correct locking) and file-based assets, but database and log-heavy components need block storage for performance and support. The design must add block storage.
Correct: identify the risk and add block storage.
The team adds ODF on dedicated storage nodes using local SSDs to provide RBD block volumes.
Storage gaps are architecture blockers. Raise them early.
Where should the OpenShift internal image registry store its data in a production cluster with multiple registry replicas?
Shared storage such as RWX file or object storage (S3-compatible), so all registry replicas see the same images
An RWO volume per replica with no sharing
Several registry replicas need shared backing storage. Object storage is commonly recommended; RWX file storage also works.
Correct: shared object or RWX storage.
The internal registry is backed by a NooBaa S3 bucket provided by ODF.
Registry with more than one replica = shared storage.
Why should container image registry location be considered in CP4I storage and architecture planning?
Image pulls during scaling, failover and upgrades depend on registry availability and bandwidth; a nearby, highly available registry (or mirror) reduces startup time and outage risk
Images never need to be pulled after install
Every new pod on a node without the image cached needs to pull it. During node failures or upgrades, many pulls happen at once. A local, resilient registry or mirror improves recovery time.
Correct: registry availability affects scale and recovery.
Wrong: images are not in PVCs.
During a zone outage, 40 pods rescheduled at once and pulled from the in-region mirror in seconds.
Recovery time includes image pull time. Mirror close to the cluster.
Which storage type is typically used as the backup target for OpenShift API for Data Protection (OADP/Velero) backups?
An emptyDir volume in the same pod
OADP stores backup metadata and data in object storage (S3-compatible or supported cloud object stores), ideally outside the protected cluster or region.
OADP backs up cp4i-prod namespaces to an S3 bucket in a different region.
Backups must live outside the failure domain they protect.
What does a CSI VolumeSnapshot provide, and what is its key limitation for disaster recovery?

A point-in-time snapshot of a volume taken by the storage system; snapshots often reside on the same storage system, so they must be copied elsewhere (for example by a data mover) to protect against storage or site loss
A full off-site backup by default

Snapshots are fast but usually local to the storage system. For DR, snapshot data must be exported to independent storage. Application consistency (quiescing or using application backups) must also be considered.
Correct: fast, but local; copy off-site for DR.
OADP's data mover copies CSI snapshot contents to S3 in the DR region.
Snapshot is not the same as a backup until the data leaves the storage system.
A team plans to rely solely on CSI volume snapshots of running queue manager, Kafka and API Connect database volumes for backup. What is the MAIN risk, and what is the better approach?

Crash-consistent snapshots of active systems may not be cleanly recoverable or may be inconsistent across replicas; use each product's supported backup mechanism (for example API Connect backups, MQ configuration backup plus replication, Kafka geo-replication) and OADP for Kubernetes resources and suitable volumes
There is no risk; snapshots are always application-consistent

Product-aware backups capture consistent state. Generic volume snapshots of busy databases, logs or replicated systems risk inconsistency. Combine product mechanisms with OADP for resource definitions.
API Connect uses its built-in database backups to S3; Kafka uses MirrorMaker 2; OADP captures CRs and Secrets.
For each capability, ask what its supported backup and restore method is.
Which CP4I component is typically STATELESS and does not need persistent storage for its runtime data?
An ACE integration runtime that receives BARs from a URL or image and keeps no local state
An MQ Native HA queue manager

ACE runtimes are generally stateless: flows and configuration come from BARs and configuration objects, and state is held externally in queues and databases. Brokers, queue managers and databases persist data.
Correct: ACE runtimes are typically stateless.
Wrong: MQ persists messages and logs.
ACE runtimes scale and restart freely with no PVCs.
Stateless components are easier to scale and recover.
A developer deployed a QueueManager with ephemeral storage for a test. After a pod restart, all queues and messages are gone. Why?
Ephemeral storage lives only for the pod's lifetime; queue manager data was lost when the pod was recreated
MQ deletes queues on restart by design

Ephemeral storage is fine for disposable tests but not for data that must survive restarts. Queue definitions supplied by MQSC ConfigMaps are recreated at startup, but messages and runtime changes are lost.
Definitions from the MQSC ConfigMap reappeared after the restart, but all test messages were lost.
Why does a Flink-based Event Processing deployment need durable storage for checkpoints and savepoints?
To recover job state after failures or upgrades without reprocessing from scratch or losing aggregation state
Flink periodically checkpoints operator state. Durable, typically shared, storage lets jobs resume from the last checkpoint after failures and allows savepoints for upgrades.
Correct: state recovery needs durable checkpoints.
After a TaskManager crash, the job resumes from a 1-minute-old checkpoint with exactly-once state.
Stateful stream processing = checkpoints on durable storage.
After a cluster-wide storage outage and recovery, some Kafka partitions show under-replicated status for hours. What is the MOST likely reason, and what should be done?

Replicas are catching up from leaders; monitor replication progress (under-replicated partitions, ISR shrink and expand), verify broker disk throughput, and avoid restarting brokers repeatedly while they recover
Data is permanently lost; delete the topics
After disruption, followers re-sync large amounts of data. Under-replicated partitions decline as replicas catch up. Disk and network throughput determine how quickly.
URPs fell from 340 to 0 over 90 minutes as followers caught up at 200 MB/s.
Under-replicated partitions = a resilience gap. Alert on them and track recovery.
Which statement about data encryption at rest for CP4I persistent volumes is MOST accurate?
Encryption at rest is generally provided by the storage layer (for example ODF encryption, cloud disk encryption with KMS), complemented by application-level protection such as MQ AMS where required
Kubernetes encrypts all PVs by default
Encryption at rest is impossible in containers
Storage-level encryption with key management protects volumes. Application-level encryption (for example AMS for MQ payloads) adds protection against privileged access.
Correct: storage-layer encryption plus application-level options.
ODF cluster-wide encryption with an external KMS meets the bank's at-rest requirement.
At rest -> storage encryption plus KMS. In transit -> TLS. End to end -> AMS.
A cloud deployment uses zonal block volumes (for example AWS EBS). What must the architect consider for MQ Native HA and Kafka brokers?
Each replica's volume is tied to its zone, so replicas should be spread one per zone, with enough node capacity in each zone for pods to reschedule within the same zone after node failures
Zonal volumes support RWX across zones
Only one zone can be used
Zonal disks cannot attach across zones. Spreading replicas across zones gives zone resilience, and capacity in each zone lets a pod reschedule next to its volume.
Correct: zone-pinned volumes need per-zone capacity.
Each zone keeps a spare worker so a failed node's Kafka broker can restart near its EBS volume.
Zonal storage means stateful pods are zone-bound.
Which Kubernetes object represents an actual piece of provisioned storage in the cluster?
A PV is the cluster resource representing provisioned storage. PVCs request it and StorageClasses describe how to provision it.
PV pvc-3f2a... is bound to claim data-qm1-ibm-mq-0.
PV = supply. PVC = demand. StorageClass = recipe.
